name: Siege of Jerusalem (1099)
info: Crusaders from Western Europe besieged Fatimid-held Jerusalem from 7 June to 15 July 1099, took it by assault with siege towers and a ram, massacred thousands of its people, and soon founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

facts.date: 7 June to 15 July 1099; a first assault failed on 13 June and the city was entered on 15 July
facts.place: Jerusalem, then under Fatimid rule, in the Levant
facts.sides: Crusaders of the First Crusade under leaders including Raymond of Toulouse, Godfrey of Lorraine, Robert of Normandy, Robert of Flanders and Tancred, with 12,000 to 14,000 men reaching the city, of whom 1,200 to 1,300 were cavalry; the Fatimid garrison under the governor Iftikhar ad-Dawla, roughly a thousand Arab and Sudanese troops and some 400 Egyptian elite cavalry
facts.outcome: The crusaders entered the city on 15 July and thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred. Godfrey of Bouillon became Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri a week later, and a Fatimid army was beaten at Ascalon in August.

t: The crusaders had too few men to surround the city, and a first assault on 13 June failed for lack of siege engines.
Timber and materials from ships that reached Jaffa let the crusaders build two siege towers, a ram and ladders in almost three weeks, and the city was entered on 15 July.
Modern estimates put the dead of the siege and massacre at between 3,000 and 10,000, far below the 70,000 or 100,000 given by some contemporary Arab sources.
dyk: The city's water came from deep cisterns, while the crusaders had only the spring of En-Gihon, whose flow dropped considerably in summer; most wells and cisterns near the city had been made unusable.
ev: Pope Urban II calls for a crusade at the Council of Clermont
Antioch falls to the crusaders, who then defeat a Seljuk relief army led by Kerbogha
The army reaches Jerusalem on 7 June and its first assault, on 13 June, fails
Crusaders march barefoot to the Mount of Olives on 8 July after a vision reported by Peter Desiderius
The final assault begins on 14 July and crusaders enter the city on 15 July, followed by a massacre
Godfrey of Bouillon is made Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri on 22 July
Godfrey defeats a Fatimid army at the Battle of Ascalon on 12 August
Baldwin is crowned the first King of Jerusalem on Christmas day

sections.background:
In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at the Council of Clermont. Besides aiding Byzantium, which the Seljuks threatened, its goal was to reach the Holy Land and liberate Jerusalem. The crusaders left Constantinople in April 1097 and reached northern Syria in the autumn. Baldwin of Boulogne marched east and in the spring of 1098 founded the County of Edessa, while the main army besieged Antioch from October 1097. After the city fell in June 1098 and a Seljuk relief army under Kerbogha was beaten, the advance came to a standstill.

Rivalry between Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond IV of Toulouse, epidemics and shortages of supplies delayed it further. Raymond took command and resumed the march south in January 1099. Following the coast, the troops avoided long sieges of fortified cities and instead made agreements with local Muslim rulers or paid tribute. At the end of May the army left the coast at Jaffa and reached the neighbourhood of Jerusalem on 7 June.

The city had been out of Christian control since the Muslim conquest of the Levant in 637. It had been held for a century first by the Seljuk Turks and later by the Egyptian Fatimids, who had ruled it since the 10th century.
sections.forces:
The crusader army had been estimated at 20,000 to 75,000 troops assembled at Nicaea. Between 12,000 and 14,000 reached Jerusalem on 7 June, among them 1,200 to 1,300 cavalry. The garrison comprised roughly a thousand Arab and Sudanese troops and some 400 Egyptian elite cavalry under the governor, Iftikhar ad-Dawla. He had denied the crusaders water, food and wood near the city, expelled Syrian Christians who might sympathise with them and allowed the Jews to stay. He had all available timber and rope used for more mangonels and ordered bags of straw to be lowered on ropes beside the walls to soften the impact of stones.

The walls were about four kilometres long, three metres thick and 15 metres high, with five major gates each guarded by a pair of towers. Steep valleys protected three sides, and only the north wall and the south-west over Mount Zion offered ground favourable to an attacker. A deep ditch dug by Seljuk governors ringed much of the city, and an outer wall just inside it, linked to the city at several points, was meant to block the low flight of stones thrown by mangonels.

With too few men to besiege the whole city, the crusaders concentrated on the approachable sectors. Robert of Normandy held the north wall opposite the Gate of Flowers, with Robert of Flanders facing the Gate of the Column. Godfrey of Lorraine and Tancred covered the north-west corner down to the Jaffa Gate, and Raymond of Toulouse stood to the south, moving up to Mount Zion after two or three days. The eastern and south-eastern sectors were left unguarded.
sections.course:
According to Raymond of Aguilers, a prophecy of an old hermit led to the first attack: if the crusaders attacked on 13 June until the ninth hour, the city would fall to them. The army improvised equipment overnight and, despite early success, the attack failed. Two days later the leaders met and concluded that the situation favoured the defenders. Thirst and ambushes while seeking water were taking lives, and rumours said the Cairo vizier al-Afdal was gathering a relief army, which left about a fortnight to take the city.

On 17 June the crusaders learned that English and Genoese ships had reached Jaffa, bringing materials for siege equipment. Timber was found over 50 kilometres away near Nablus. Under Guglielmo Embriaco and Gaston of Béarn they built two wheel-mounted siege towers, an iron-headed ram, scaling ladders and wattle screens in almost three weeks. On 8 July the whole army walked barefoot to the Mount of Olives, led by bishops and priests, after Peter Desiderius reported a vision of the legate Adhémar calling for a fast and a procession.

The assault began in the night of 13 to 14 July, with the main attack from Mount Zion and on the eastern part of the north wall and a feint at the north-west angle. By evening the ram had pierced the north wall, but it stuck, and the general attack was stopped. At midday on Friday 15 July the attack resumed; the tower was pushed against the wall and the crusaders entered the city. Albert of Aachen says a golden cross was placed on top of the tower.
sections.aftermath:
The crusaders' losses in the final attack were heavy, probably a fifth or a quarter of the Western armies. After the city fell, thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred. Accounts by Christians, Muslims and Jews all describe women and children not being spared, and eyewitnesses say the blood on the Temple Mount reached to the ankles or the reins. Jews who had defended the city alongside the Muslims were burned alive in their synagogue. Albert of Aachen mentions a second mass execution days later of those first spared for ransom.

Some Muslims withdrew to the Tower of David, and after negotiations Iftikhar and others left safely for Ascalon. Jews were also spared if they left the city voluntarily. Muslim holy sites on the Temple Mount were converted into Christian shrines. Raymond of Aguilers writes of heads, hands and feet lying in the houses and streets, and of men and knights running to and fro over the corpses.

There are no reliable figures for the dead. Contemporary Arab sources give 70,000 or even 100,000, which is unrealistic against a population of about 30,000, and modern estimates range from 3,000 to 10,000. On 17 July a council met on the Dome of the Rock about who should be king. On 22 July Godfrey of Bouillon was made Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri and declined the title of king, refusing to wear a crown of gold where Christ wore one of thorns. He defeated a Fatimid army at Ascalon on 12 August.
sections.sources:
The siege is known chiefly from Latin chronicles. Raymond of Aguilers, the anonymous authors known as the Anonymi and Albert of Aachen are called eyewitnesses; Ralph of Caen also reports events of the siege. William of Tyre wrote about 90 years after the massacre. Christian, Muslim and Jewish accounts all describe the bloodshed, though the Christian eyewitnesses regarded it as a triumph of God and express no regret, which later accounts such as William's do.

Much is disputed or told by one chronicler only. Raymond of Aguilers is the source for the hermit's prophecy, and Albert of Aachen for the golden cross and for a local Christian who showed the crusaders where timber lay. Ralph of Caen has Tancred finding a cave with about 400 beams, left perhaps by the Fatimids. Visions such as that of Peter Desiderius are reported as what he claimed. The death toll is the largest uncertainty. Arab figures of 70,000 or 100,000 are not credible against a population of about 30,000, and modern estimates run from 3,000 to 10,000.
sections.legacy:
The capture of Jerusalem marked the successful end of the First Crusade and led soon afterwards to the founding of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Godfrey of Bouillon, who had played the most fundamental role in the conquest, took the title of advocate of the Holy Sepulchre and held it until his death on 18 July 1100. His brother Baldwin was asked to come to Jerusalem to take over his inheritance, in order to prevent Daibert of Pisa from taking the city. Baldwin arrived in November 1100 and was crowned on Christmas day in the Church of the Nativity as the first King of Jerusalem.

The fall of the city also gave Christian rulers control of Jerusalem for the first time since 637. The Temple Mount's Muslim holy sites became Christian shrines.

The accounts agree on the bloodshed. Atrocities against the inhabitants of cities taken by storm were normal in ancient and medieval warfare, by Christians and Muslims alike. The crusaders had already done so at Antioch, and the Fatimids had done so at Taormina, at Rometta and at Tyre. The eyewitnesses saw the bloodshed as a triumph of God, not the killing of innocents.

summary: From 7 June to 15 July 1099 the crusaders besieged Fatimid-held Jerusalem, took it with siege towers after a failed first assault, and massacred thousands of its Muslims and Jews. Modern estimates of the dead run from 3,000 to 10,000. The Kingdom of Jerusalem followed.

notes: Article contradicts itself on the walls: Prelude gives 3 m thick and 15 m high stone walls; the Siege section says the inner wall was 12 to 15 m but not very thick. I gave the Prelude figures and left the 'not very thick' out.
Garrison: article says 'roughly some thousand Arab and Sudanese troops'; I wrote 'roughly a thousand'.
The article gives the crusader assembly at Nicaea as 20,000 to 75,000; I wrote it as an estimate of troops assembled.

Left out: Peter Bartholomew, Arnulf of Chocques, the Provencal tensions, the Christians' treatment inside the city, the mirror signalling on the Mount of Olives (garbled: 'reflectors'), the Fatimid horse figures beyond the 400 cavalry.

'Godfrey of Lorraine' and 'Godfrey of Lotharingia' both appear; I used Lorraine for the leader and Bouillon where the article does. 'Governor al-Dawla managed to escape' conflicts with later 'Iftikhar ... safe departure to Ascalon'; I told only the negotiated departure.
The sentence 'Being part of the Jewish quarter Fatimid archers ... supported by local civilians' is garbled; left out. 'Jews ... burned alive in their synagogue' is as the article states.
In the legacy section I wrote 'first time since 637' from the lead (out of Christian control since 637).
Raymond of Aguilers' quotation is paraphrased, not quoted.
